---
title: "Effects by group and many tests"
description: >
  How to get the effect for each event time, how to keep some treated cells
  out of the estimate, and how to adjust p-values for many tests.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
source("_setup.R")
```

::: {.key-points}
Key points

- `trop_effects()` gives the mean effect of a group of treated cells. A group
  can be all cells with the same event time. The event time is the number of
  periods since the treatment started.
- The band of `trop_effects()` covers all groups together. An interval covers
  one group only.
- The argument `target` keeps some treated cells out of the estimate. Use it
  when the treatment is not complete in those cells.
- `trop_boot_rows()` and `trop_stepdown()` adjust the p-values of many tests.
  All tests must use the same bootstrap rows.
- This article uses practice data. The data have a known effect.
:::

## A practice panel

The panel has 40 units and 20 periods. Twelve units get the treatment. The
start of the treatment is different for each unit. This is a staggered
design. The true effect is 1 in each treated cell.

```{r data}
library(fasttrop)
panel <- trop_simulate(n_units = 40, n_periods = 20, n_treated = 12, n_post = 6,
                       design = "staggered", seed = 1)
head(panel)
```

The paper proves the triple robustness property only for a block design.
Thus, `trop()` gives a warning message for a staggered design. This article
hides that message. Read the article [What TROP can and cannot
do](limits.html) before you use a staggered design.

To keep the build fast, the fit uses fixed tuning parameters. The bootstrap
has 100 draws. A real analysis must use more draws.

```{r fit, warning = FALSE}
lambda <- c(time = 0.2, unit = 0.5, nn = 0.5)
fit <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "d", unit = "unit", time = "time",
            lambda = lambda, n_boot = 100, seed = 1)
fit
```

## The effect for each event time

The function `trop_effects()` starts from a fit. The argument `by` selects the
groups. The choices are `"event_time"`, `"cohort"`, `"time"`, `"unit"`, and
`"overall"`. You can also give a matrix with one group number for each cell.

```{r effects}
ev <- trop_effects(fit, by = "event_time")
ev
```

The estimate of a group is the mean of the effects of its cells. The column
`n_cells` gives the number of cells. The function uses the bootstrap draws of
the fit. Thus, the draws of all groups come from the same resamples of units.
This is necessary for the band.

```{r effects-fig, echo = FALSE, fig.asp = 0.55, fig.cap = "The effect for each event time of the practice panel. The points are the estimates, the thick bars are the 95% intervals for one event time, and the light band covers all event times together. The dashed line is the true effect of 1.", fig.alt = "A chart with the event time on the horizontal axis and the estimated effect on the vertical axis. Teal points show the estimate for each event time. Thick teal bars show the interval for each point. A wider light teal band shows the simultaneous band. A dashed grey line marks the true effect of 1."}
df <- as.data.frame(ev)
ggplot(df, aes(event_time, estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = ft_col[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "22") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = band.low, ymax = band.high), fill = ft_col[["teal_light"]], alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), colour = ft_col[["teal"]], linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(colour = ft_col[["teal_dark"]], size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = df$event_time) +
  labs(x = "Event time (periods since the start of the treatment)", y = "Effect")
```

Use the band to read the pattern of effects over time. If the band excludes 0
at every event time, then you have evidence for an effect at every event
time. An interval for one event time gives no such evidence. If you compare
many intervals, one of them can exclude 0 by chance.

The band is a sup-t band. Its critical value is a quantile of the largest
absolute standardized draw over the groups. The band is accurate only with
many draws. With a small number of draws, the band is not accurate. With one
group, the band columns are `NA`.

## Keep cells out of the estimate

Sometimes the treatment is not complete in some treated cells. For example, a
rollout can start in a period but reach all users only some periods later. The
argument `target` keeps such cells out of the estimate.

Give `target` as a column of the data with the values `TRUE` and `FALSE`. A
cell with `FALSE` stays in the panel, but it is not in the estimate. In the
next fit, the cells in the last 2 periods are outside of the target.

```{r target, warning = FALSE}
panel$in_target <- panel$time <= 18
fit_t <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "d", unit = "unit", time = "time",
              lambda = lambda, target = "in_target", se = "none")
c(all_cells = coef(fit), target_only = coef(fit_t))
c(treated_cells = fit_t$n_treated_cells, outside_target = fit_t$n_excluded_cells)
```

The two estimates can be different. The second estimate does not use the
cells in the last 2 periods. The result `n_excluded_cells` counts the treated
cells that are not in the estimate. The printed fit shows the same number.

Use `target` only for a reason that is not in the outcomes. If you choose
the target after you see the effects, the estimate is not correct.

## Adjust the p-values of many tests

A test for one event time is not enough when you test many event times or
many outcomes. With many tests, one of them can be significant by chance.
`trop_stepdown()` uses the method of Romano and Wolf (2005). It controls the
probability of one or more false rejections.

The method must have the joint bootstrap distribution of all estimates. Thus, all
estimates must use the same resampled units. To do this, make the rows once
with `trop_boot_rows()`. Then give the rows to each fit.

The example has two outcomes. The first outcome is `y`. Its true effect is 1.
The second outcome is `y0`, the outcome without the treatment. Its true effect
is 0.

```{r stepdown, warning = FALSE}
W <- tapply(panel$d, list(panel$unit, panel$time), sum)
rows <- trop_boot_rows(W, n_boot = 100, seed = 2)

fit_y <- trop(panel, "y", "d", "unit", "time", lambda = lambda, boot_rows = rows)
fit_0 <- trop(panel, "y0", "d", "unit", "time", lambda = lambda, boot_rows = rows)

res <- trop_stepdown(list(effect = fit_y, no_effect = fit_0))
res
```

The column `p_raw` is the p-value of one test. The column `p_adj` is the
adjusted p-value. An adjusted p-value is never smaller than the raw p-value.
You can also give `trop_effects()` objects, for example to test each event
time. The objects must have the same bootstrap rows. If they do not, the
function gives an error.

```{r stepdown-events}
ev_0 <- trop_effects(fit_0, by = "event_time")
trop_stepdown(ev_0)
```

With `strata`, `trop_boot_rows()` resamples the units inside groups that you
define, for example the waves of a rollout. Each draw keeps the number of
treated units and the number of untreated units in each group. The argument
`resample = "controls"` keeps the treated units fixed and resamples only the
untreated units.

## Put the grid on the scale of the outcome

The grid of `trop_grid()` uses fixed values. The best values of the
unit parameter and of the nuclear norm parameter depend on the scale of the
outcome. An outcome in large units can make the search choose the edge of the
grid.

The function `trop_grid_scaled()` makes a grid that follows the scale of the
data. It divides the values of `unit` by the median distance between two
units. It multiplies the finite values of `nn` by the root mean square of the
residuals of a two-way fixed effects fit. The values of `time` do not change.

```{r grid}
Y <- tapply(panel$y, list(panel$unit, panel$time), sum)
g1 <- trop_grid_scaled(Y, W)
g100 <- trop_grid_scaled(100 * Y, W)
rbind(outcome = unlist(attr(g1, "scales")), outcome_times_100 = unlist(attr(g100, "scales")))
```

The scales are 100 times larger for the outcome in larger units. Thus, the
same relative grid applies to both outcomes. To use the scaled grid in a fit,
set `grid = "auto"`.

When the cross-validation chooses a value at the edge of the grid,
`trop()` gives a warning message. A value outside of the grid can fit better.
Use a wider grid or `grid = "auto"`. The result `cv$boundary` names the
values at the edge.

## Remove the unit means

The argument `demean = TRUE` subtracts the mean of each unit before the fit.
A unit effect absorbs a constant for each unit. Thus, the effects do not
change when the unit parameter is 0. When the unit parameter is more than 0,
the unit distances do not include the difference in the level of the units.

## Record the version

Each fit stores the version of fasttrop, and the commit when the package comes
from GitHub, in `fit$package`. The summary prints them. Keep this line with
your results. It tells which version made them.

```{r package}
fit$package
```

::: {.limit-box}
Limits

- As in `trop()`, the bootstrap keeps the tuning parameters fixed. It does not
  include the variation that comes from the selection of the tuning
  parameters.
- `trop_effects()` runs the draws one after another in R. With many draws and
  many cells, it can be slower than the bootstrap of `trop()`.
- The sup-t band and the stepdown p-values are accurate only with many
  draws. Use at least several hundred.
- `trop_effects()` is for the local method. The global method has no
  effects for each cell.
- `target` is for the local method.
:::

## References

Romano, J. P., and Wolf, M. (2005). Stepwise multiple testing as formalized
data snooping. *Econometrica*, 73(4), 1237-1282.
